name: Lena Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the electricity company's new connection crew where housing is going up beyond the old service road. My two-year technical diploma taught me the drawings; years in the trench taught me where they lie. At 43 I enjoy teaching an apprentice to measure a cable run, and I get tired of developers changing the access at dawn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and where does AI fit in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs delivery vehicles, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage, about four months of expenses saved and my lineworker pay is around the usual rate; there are some other utility crews nearby. I use AI every morning to sort the parts and job order, but I check the drawings and ground before buying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the AI rush was oversold, but my daily parts list still saves a phone call. An apprentice has to fit the connector, test the line and own the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead job building new connections looks steady, and my partner's vehicle repair work is hands-on too. Four months of expenses in savings give us some room, though the mortgage means we keep watching cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the new housing connection crew and use the AI list I already run each morning. Before ordering, I'll compare its cable sizes with the engineer's drawing and ask the apprentice to measure the actual trench route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our pay. I would be glad if the useful little tool stayed useful and the grand claims quieted down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the parts tool get a job wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool once suggested a shorter cable because it missed the bend round the pump house. We measured the route again and ordered the longer length, avoiding a wasted installation day. The AI parts list missed the bend around the pump house; our crew measured before ordering cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my daughter to learn the measurement, not only the app. The app can change; the habit of checking the real route will follow her into any trade.

say: **AI parts lists** can save time, but the crew must measure and fit every connection.
An **apprentice** should learn the real cable route before trusting a generated length.
think: My **lead lineworker role** and my partner's vehicle repair shifts look steady.
A **four-month reserve** helps with ordinary setbacks while we keep paying the mortgage.
do: **Keep** leading new housing connections and using the daily AI parts list.
**Check** generated cable sizes against drawings and a measured trench route.
feel: **Calm** about pay and pleased to keep the small useful tool.
S0.quote: The AI parts list missed the bend around the pump house; our crew measured before ordering cable.
fieldNote: She uses AI **every day** but demands measurements before committing material.
Two hands-on household jobs and a **four-month reserve** underpin her calm in the plateau.

steps.text: Keep leading new housing connections and daily parts planning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may handle buying, booking and drawings sooner than a robot handles a muddy connection pit. I'd ask the electricity company to keep a crew lead's right to correct the order when a developer changes the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My field job still has a reason to exist, but fewer buyers at the office could mean more checking pushed onto us. I might gain responsibility without extra pay, and four months' savings will not cover a long household income drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll run the new company planner beside my own board on three connection jobs and mark every wrong access or cable length. If the trial works, I'll teach my crew the corrections on paid time and keep a record of any extra hours it takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the quiet transfer of work, not convinced my crew will be cut. I am willing to use a proved planner, not absorb its mistakes for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a drawing misses a moved drain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the order and phone the engineer before the cable lorry leaves. A power-line drawing that ignores a moved drain can waste my crew's whole day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask to be paid for extra checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the supervisor the three marked orders and the hours spent fixing them. If the company wants a crew lead to check software, it needs to put that time on the roster.

say: **AI buying and drawing** may change before robots can build new power connections.
A **crew lead** must be able to correct orders when the ground changes.
think: My **field work** should continue, though software errors could become unpaid crew checks.
Four months of **savings** would not cover an extended household wage loss.
do: **Test** the company planner beside my board on three connection jobs.
**Log** wrong access, cable lengths and extra checking hours for the supervisor.
feel: **Uneasy** about added responsibility without paid time.
S1.quote: A power-line drawing that ignores a moved drain can waste my crew's whole day.
fieldNote: She is open to a planner after a **three-job trial** with measurable errors.
Her concern is **unpaid checking** moving from the buying office to the field crew.

steps.text: Test company AI planner on three connection jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew thinking AI by 2028 might design and order the connections before we arrive. Capable robots around 2031 could then do the physical cable and pole work, so I would ask the company for honest crew numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn equipment quickly and maybe help test it, but that does not guarantee a paid place. My partner's vehicle work may also face robots later, and four months of savings would not support a long mortgage gap. My quick robot training would not turn four months of savings into a mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask management for separate 2028 office and 2031 field plans and apply for a paid installation-robot trial if one opens. We'll postpone a new kitchen floor and save the amount we would pay monthly for it from future wages until the reserve reaches six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can see things to do. I would not tell the family we're ruined on the strength of a scenario when we still have two wages and some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children the floor can wait, and that school and meals stay first. I would also say I have asked about my crew's future instead of pretending to know the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the robot trial worth joining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real trial would let me operate the safety stop and keep my usual lineworker wage. I would not leave my crew for an unpaid viewing day or buy a course without a job attached.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes design and orders before physical line robots arrive around 2031.
The electricity company should publish **field crew numbers** before selling a new machine.
think: I might earn a **paid trial role**, but learning quickly does not guarantee a vacancy.
Four months of **savings** cannot cover a long loss of either household wage.
do: **Ask** management for separate office and field staffing plans.
**Join** a paid robot installation trial if offered with normal wages and stop controls.
**Save** monthly kitchen-floor money from future wages until six months are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about possible crew cuts, with some time and options.
S2.quote: My quick robot training would not turn four months of savings into a mortgage plan.
fieldNote: Her early adoption of AI does not remove the **income risk** from later field robots.
A trial requires **normal wages and controls**, not observation alone.
New saving comes from **future pay** once the kitchen floor is postponed.

steps.text: Ask management for 2028 office and 2031 field staffing plans
Join paid installation-robot trial if offered with wages and controls
Save monthly kitchen-floor money from future wages until six months covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a few more years lets us test robots on a real connection site before field machines arrive around 2034. Thinking AI in 2031 will change plans sooner, and I would rather be the person who spots the bad drawing than inherit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could still lead a crew that checks robot installations, if there are paid posts. If the company simply reduces crews, I'd look at other electricity employers nearby, but I would not move on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the company's AI connection drawings against five completed jobs this year, then present the errors to our engineer. If a paid robot controls course with field practice opens after a successful trial, I'll enrol while retaining my lead wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can work with five years. I do not need to love every new machine to want my crew trained before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the engineer from those five jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd circle the wrong cable size and the missing drain on each drawing, then take the engineer to one finished site. A clean AI drawing will not persuade me as much as a real power-line trench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you enrol in the controls course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need the course to be paid, scheduled during work and connected to a real lead or inspection vacancy. Otherwise I'd keep my crew shifts and use the training time on current safety work.

say: **Five completed sites** can expose drawing errors before 2034 field robots arrive.
**Paid controls training** should come with field practice and a real role.
think: A robot-checking **lead post** might suit me, but it has not been offered.
Other nearby **utilities** are a fallback only if this company actually cuts crews.
do: **Compare** five AI connection drawings with finished sites and show errors to the engineer.
**Enrol** in a paid robot controls course after a successful trial if field practice and a real role are offered.
feel: **Anxious** about crew size, with enough time to test and learn.
S3.quote: A clean AI drawing will not persuade me as much as a real power-line trench.
fieldNote: She tests **AI drawings** against five built sites rather than assuming the output is correct.
Enrolment requires a **paid course**, field practice and a connected vacancy.

steps.text: Compare five AI drawings with built connection sites
Enrol in paid robot controls course after successful trial if field practice and role offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to give apprentices a firm grounding in connections before robots arrive around 2039. Thinking AI in 2036 changes the drawings first; I want the company to show the crew the work it expects after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 56 at the robot date, and I might want to teach installations or inspect finished work. That only helps if there is a paid post, and I still expect to have mortgage costs at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading connections and renew my diploma-related line safety tickets. Each year I'll ask for actual paid trainer or inspection vacancies and review our mortgage balance with my partner before applying for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to plan across a decade, though I will miss the days when a crew builds the whole run itself. I want the children to see careful work, whatever tools do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son about an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son to try an apprenticeship day before choosing a trade and to learn how the connection is tested. I would not tell him a machine makes a skill worthless or safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a trainer post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trainer post would need full pay, real apprentice hours and responsibility for safe site work. I would not leave the lead roster for a ceremonial title. A power-line trainer title without full pay and apprentice hours would be decoration, not a job.

say: **Apprentices** need connection and testing practice before field robots arrive around 2039.
**2036 thinking AI** changes drawings ahead of physical line installation.
think: A paid **trainer or inspection post** might suit me at 56 if one exists.
Our **mortgage** still requires a proper wage, even with a decade to prepare.
do: **Renew** line safety tickets and keep leading new connections.
**Check** paid trainer and inspection vacancies annually before any job application.
feel: **Calm** about preparation time, with some sadness about how crews may change.
S4.quote: A power-line trainer title without full pay and apprentice hours would be decoration, not a job.
fieldNote: Her longer runway makes **paid teaching** plausible, yet she insists on a real vacancy.
She keeps **apprentice practice** and mortgage-covering pay central to the plan.

steps.text: Renew line safety tickets and keep leading new connections
Check paid trainer and inspection vacancies annually

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the planning change would arrive fast, then capable installation robots could cut crew hours around 2031. Honest numbers for field crews and paid controls training tied to a real role would let me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company will pay a lead worker to correct a wrong machine drawing. The apprentices see me stop the job when a cable size is wrong, and that is part of the work. A safe connection is worth a day more than a fast mistake. A safe power-line connection is worth a day more than a fast mistake.

headlineQuote: A safe power-line connection is worth a day more than a fast mistake.
portrait: **Lena**, 43, leads new electricity connections and teaches apprentices after a two-year technical diploma.
She uses **AI daily** for materials and scheduling, then checks cable routes against the ground.
Her **four-month reserve**, typical pay, mortgage and partner's vehicle repair job give some flexibility but limit a long income gap.
She wants **paid robot controls** and real trainer posts before changing her lead crew role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives limited time before installation robots around 2031 might reduce crew hours.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **field crew numbers** and paid controls training tied to a real role would guide her plan.
